newsitem.title: USA: World Bank backs IMF on Kenya corruption concern.
newsitem.headline: World Bank backs IMF on Kenya corruption concern.

text.p: The World Bank has already delayed paying part of a loan to Kenya and will find it hard to hand over the money until Nairobi addresses concerns on widespread corruption, a World Bank official said on Monday.

The official, who asked not to be named, said the bank shared the concerns of the International Monetary Fund, which halted its Kenya loan programme on July 31 complaining that government was not doing enough to stamp out graft.

"The second tranche of our structural adjustment loan had been suspended because policy conditions (on privatisation) had not been met, but we would find it difficult to release this money until the IMF programme is back on track," he said.
He said the Kenyan government had received a first tranche of the loan last year, but the second tranche, totalling just over $71 million, had not been paid.
An energy sector loan, approved by the World Bank board in June, could also be in doubt because the IMF had singled out the sector as one suspected of mismanagement.

"The IMF cited suspected mismanagement in the energy sector when it allowed its loan to lapse, and given that...it is most likely that we will not make this credit effective," the World Bank official said.

The IMF's decision to halt its Kenyan loan programme sent financial markets in Nairobi into a tailspin as foreign investors, also worried about political violence in the African state, pulled funds out.
The shilling fell 1.64 percent to a commercial mean rate of 70 to the dollar on Monday.

The World Bank official said its credits for social and environmental programmes were still being paid, although government cash shortages due to the IMF decision to halt its $205 million loan meant loans for development projects could lapse if Nairobi could no longer fund its share.
He said the bank, which highlighted the need for good government in a major report released in June, was watching closely to ensure that the money was properly spent.

The IMF, which is worried about the impact of corruption on economic growth prospects, has said talks on a loan can only start after the government shows it is serious about the anti-corruption fight.

New IMF guidelines on corruption say staff can recommend halting a loan if they suspect poor governance is hurting a country's economic performance or threatening the implementation of an IMF reform plan.
